core.text: To report that something *will* happen, Latin uses **the future infinitive (the 'going to' form: venturum esse)**: the future participle plus *esse*. He says *sē epistulam scrīptūrum esse* — that he will write a letter. The participle agrees with the accusative subject of the reported clause, so *sē … scrīptūram esse* for a woman, *eōs … factūrōs esse* for several men. Latin name: *īnfīnītīvus futūrī*.
*She hopes that he will come*: English keeps a future verb inside the *that*-clause. Latin puts the future on the infinitive instead.
Future participle (accusative, agreeing) + esse. Esse is often left out: dīcit sē ventūrum. Sum has futūrum esse or the one-word fore.

invented.la: Mārcus prōmittit sē bonum puerum futūrum esse.
invented.en: Marcus promises that he will be a good boy.

core.text: Three infinitives, three times. *Scrībere* — is writing (same time); **the perfect infinitive (the 'to have done' form)** *scrīpsisse* — wrote (earlier); *scrīptūrum esse* — will write (later). The -ūr- marks the future, the -isse the past.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 23) point out that English has nothing like this and translates with a *that*-clause and *will* or *would*: *audīvistis nōs profectūrōs esse* — you heard that we were going to leave. *Fore* is the short form of *futūrum esse*: after *spērō* — I hope — *eum brevī sānum fore*, that he will soon be well.

The future passive infinitive is supine + *īrī* (*laudātum īrī* — to be going to be praised); it never changes its ending and is rare. Ørberg shows it in cap. XXIII, where Aemilia fears her son *ā patre verberātum īrī*.
